introduction: “Things are known by their opposites.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses the old maxim in several ways. It describes experience: this world alternates plenty and hardship, youth and age, and we value sight by seeing blindness. It supports an argument for God: limitation implies the unlimited, weakness power. It helps explain why the light of a revelation appears in the darkest night. And it comes with a correction: many opposites are not two things but a thing and its absence. Darkness is the lack of light, oppression the lack of justice; in the sun there is no darkness at all. The moral contrast, however, stays sharp, and the choice clear. Ecclesiastes and Ben Sira say that God “set the one over against the other.” Heraclitus, Plato’s Socrates, Shakespeare, Keats and Emily Dickinson notice the same law. Blake thought contraries necessary and good in themselves; Isaiah has God create darkness and evil; and Dostoevsky’s Ivan refuses any harmony bought with suffering.
questions: Name something you came to value only by losing it or seeing its absence. Does the maxim explain why this world “does not remain in one state”?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says darkness, poverty and oppression are absences and have no existence of their own. What difference does that make to how one works against them?
Isaiah says God creates darkness and evil; the readings say evil is non-existence. Can both be affirmed?
Ivan Karamazov gives back his ticket. Does the teaching that evil is an absence answer him, or was it never meant to?
“Limitation itself proveth the existence of the unlimited.” Is that a proof, a pointer, or a way of seeing? What would a sceptic say?
Opposites make things known, yet “you know which path to follow.” Why does knowing by contrast not make good and evil equal partners?

outside.why: “Things are often known by their opposites.” Ben Sira saw the pairing as the Creator’s design: good is set against evil, and life against death; so look upon all the works of the most High; and there are two and two, one against another.
Emily Dickinson: water is taught by thirst; land, by the oceans passed; transport, by throe; peace, by its battles told.
“Sometimes there is abundance and sometimes hardship.” Ecclesiastes: in the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other.
Knowledge is valued more when ignorance has been seen, sight when blindness. The banished Duke in As You Like It: sweet are the uses of adversity.
Socrates, rubbing his leg when the chain came off on his last morning: how singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it.
“Everything is made manifest through its opposite.” Heraclitus: the way up and the way down is one and the same.

Blake made a law of it and went further: without Contraries is no progression. Attraction and Repulsion, Reason and Energy, Love and Hate, are necessary to Human existence. The readings say opposites make things known. Do they also say, with Blake, that both sides are necessary and good?

Poverty, oppression and deficiency “imply non-existence and not existence”: evil is an absence. Isaiah has God claim both sides as his work: I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil. How does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s account of evil as absence read a verse like this one?

Darkness is only the absence of light, and oppression the absence of justice. Ivan Karamazov would not accept any account that makes a child’s suffering less than real: too high a price is asked for harmony; I hasten to give back my entrance ticket. What does calling evil an absence explain, and what does it leave to be done?
“Limitation itself proveth the existence of the unlimited.” Paul reasons from the made to the Maker: the invisible things of him are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.

Opposites appear, “but in reality there is no opposition”; in the sun there is no darkness, no east and west. Heraclitus: to God all things are fair and good and right, but men hold some things wrong and some right.
“Until the darkness of the darkest night appears, the lights of the Sun of Truth will not be visible.” John: the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
“You know which path to follow: you cannot be mistaken.” Moses: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life.

While the lamp burns no one remarks on it; in sudden darkness all exclaim what a good thing light is. Keats found the same law in joy itself: in the very temple of Delight veil’d Melancholy has her sovran shrine.

sirach-two-and-two-one-against-another.text: Good is set against evil, and life against death: so is the godly against the sinner, and the sinner against the godly. So look upon all the works of the most High; and there are two and two, one against another
